title: TB7-16091
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to overturn the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), which found that the Appellants were not credible because they had submitted fraudulent documents and their evidence contained material contradictions.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellants are a family of Nigerian citizens: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "Principal Appellant"), his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "female Appellant") and their children XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX (the "minor Appellants"). The Appellants made a refugee claim for two reasons. First, the Principal Appellant's family is threatening to force them to undergo rituals and to circumcise the women in the family; the Appellants' first daughter is alleged to have been forcibly circumcised and died. Second, the Principal Appellant's brother was arrested for being homosexual, and both the police and the family are seeking the Principal Appellant on suspicion that he supported his brother's behaviour.

The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to overturn the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), which found that the Appellants were not credible because they had submitted fraudulent documents and their evidence contained material contradictions. The Appellants argue that these findings are in error. They seek to admit new evidence on appeal and request that the RAD hold an oral hearing.

This appeal is dismissed. For the following reasons, I agree with the RPD that the Appellants are not credible. I confirm the determination of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

The Appellants have tendered four pieces of new evidence: a. a letter from a lawyer in Nigeria, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX;1 b. a letter purporting to be from the Nigerian police;2 c. a photograph of what looks like a sign in front of a police station;3 and d. a letter purporting to be from the Nigerian National Population Commission.4

New evidence from the person who is the subject of the appeal is only admissible if it meets one of the statutory conditions set out in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), namely that it arose after, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been expected to have presented at the time the claim was rejected.

The first three documents submitted were created after the rejection of the Appellants' claim, and in response to the RPD's decision. In this case, the Appellants could not have known prior to receiving the reasons that the RPD would find that they had submitted fraudulent documents such as police reports and birth and death certificates. The RPD drew negative inferences on the face of the documents which were not put to the Appellants. This was not in error since the irregularities were evident on the face of the documents, but I agree that the Appellants could not have known of these concerns prior to the rejection of their claim. Therefore, the first three documents do meet the statutory conditions.
I also considered, however, if the evidence is credible, relevant, and new as per Singh.5

I do not find the letters from Mr. XXXX and the police to be sufficiently credible and relevant to be admissible. The RPD found major credibility concerns with the three police reports submitted to it.6 As evaluated below in greater detail, I have not found errors with the RPD's findings. The police reports, though issued by the same station, were inconsistent in appearance and in particular in the police logo - a logo reported to be consistent across the country. The first two reports were quite lengthy, despite the Principal Appellant's statement in his Basis of Claim form that the police stated that they would not get involved. Moreover, the RAD notes that the first report was issued to an address at which the Appellants did not live at the time in question.

The new letter from the police does not address these concerns. The letter simply asserts that the first three police reports are genuine. There is no accompanying identification of the author of the report, or any additional security features that differentiate the verification letter from the other police reports. I note that the first three reports accompany this letter and have been stamped as "verified" - the stamp, however, is not specific to the police but appears the kind available where office supplies are sold. Moreover, the letter purports to be issued at the request of a lawyer on behalf of the Principal Appellant "who is still on [the police] wanted list."7 I do not find it plausible that police would produce documentation at the request of a lawyer assisting a fugitive. Since the new police letter does not address or explain the concerns with the first three reports, is produced in the same manner on letterhead similar to the first three reports, and purports to have been issued under incredible circumstances, I do not find this new letter to offer any more validity to the original three reports. It could have been created and obtained in the exact same fraudulent manner and offers nothing to refute the RPD's negative inferences. Therefore, I find that the new letter from the Nigerian police is not sufficiently credible, and since it offers nothing different or additional to enhance the probative value of the other reports, also not sufficiently new and relevant for admission.

With respect to the letter from lawyer Mr. XXXX, I find that it is coloured with the same relevance and credibility problems as the new letter from the police. In particular, it does not explain how a lawyer whose client is a fugitive from police is able to seek police assistance, or how his lawyer was able to do so on his behalf, despite apparently knowing the whereabouts of a wanted person. The value of the letter is to attest to the fact that Mr. XXXX was retained by and assisted the Appellants in getting the police letter. He cannot, independently, verify the first three police documents. His evidence is therefore also not sufficiently relevant to the issues on appeal be admissible.

I also note that the letter from the police was also submitted with what appears to be a photograph of the sign outside of a police station. The Appellants have not explained who took this photograph, when it was taken or what evidentiary value they wish assigned to it. It is not referenced in the new letter from the police, which specifically mentions an attachment of copies of the other police reports. I therefore do not find this evidence meets the criteria of subsection 110(4) - there is no explanation as to why this photograph could not have been obtained prior to the RPD's rejection of the claim. I also find in the alternative that the photograph is neither credible (without any information as to its provenance) nor relevant - that someone took this photograph and gave it to the Appellants is not evidence that the police reports or other allegations in this appeal are credible.

The Appellants also tender a letter which purports to be from the National Population Commission of Nigeria, attesting to the fact that the birth certificate for the Appellants' first daughter, XXXX, is genuine.8 The RPD found that the certificate was fraudulent, in large part because it differed in significant ways from XXXX death certificate although both documents were meant to be issued by the same institution. The letter refers to a certificate of birth (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX) issued to XXXX XXXX - this reference number does not appear anywhere on the birth certificate provided, which has a different certificate number and registry entry number.9 It is therefore unclear if the letter is referring to any document in evidence before me. The letter asserts that the certificate is valid, and states that it "must have been issued after the presentation of the necessary documents" - but does not list what documents were presented in this case or respond to any of the concerns raised by the RPD about the birth certificate. It does not list how the certificate was validated. While there is space for a telephone number to be listed, this is blank on the document. The stamp beside the signature, which is purportedly on behalf of the state director of the National Population Commission differs from the stamp of the Commission on the birth certificate.10 Finally, the letter conspicuously makes no mention at all of the death certificate, the standard form for either birth or death certificates, or why the two documents were different. For all of these reasons, I do not find that the document is sufficiently credible or, because it does not respond to the RPD's concerns, relevant to be admissible as per Singh.11 REQUEST FOR ORAL HEARING DENIED

My jurisdiction to convene an oral hearing is limited: there must be admissible new evidence that raises a serious issue of credibility, is central, and determinative.12 No new evidence has been admitted, and so no hearing can be convened. The Appellants' request for an oral hearing is denied.

The Appellants raise a single issue: whether or not the RPD's credibility findings are sustainable in relation to the birth and death certificates of the Appellants' first daughter, her omission from the Basis of Claim form (BOC), the police reports, the involvement of police, the supporting affidavits, and the weight to be given to a psychological report.

The RAD reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it.13 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard, which, in particular cases, attracts a standard of review of reasonableness.14 Unless specifically stated below, I have applied a correctness standard.

The Appellants challenge the RPD's negative credibility findings. For the following reasons, I find that the RPD did not err in its overall conclusion that the Appellants were not credible. The Appellants have not established the life or death of their first daughter

The RPD found that the Appellants had not established that they had a daughter, XXXX who died as a result of female genital mutilation for three reasons: the birth and death certificates were fraudulent, the medical report about XXXX was fraudulent, and the Appellants did not list her as a family member in their initial BOC. Birth and death certificate
The Appellants submitted a birth15 and death16 certificate for XXXX XXXX. The RPD did not find these to be genuine documents for several reasons.

First, the Principal Appellant was able to state that one of these certificates was issued on XXXX XXXX, 2001 and one on XXXX XXXX, 2003, but he could not remember which was which. The RPD did not find this to be credible, since if his daughter was born in 2001 and died in 2003, it is reasonable to expect the Principal Appellant could tell the order in which her birth and death certificate were issued. The Appellants argue this was microscopic, but appear to misunderstand the finding. They argue it is unreasonable to expect the Principal Appellant to recall the exact dates that the certificates were applied for and obtained, given the passage of time. This would be unreasonable, but this was not the RPD's finding. I see no error in this finding.

The RPD also compared the two certificates, both purportedly issued by the National Population Commission, and found notable differences. The sizes were different, the logos of the National Birth & Death Registration Programme were different, the crests were different, the watermarks were different, the stamp of the issuing office is different, and certain standard features of the documents were different such as how the applicable law is referenced. These findings, given that they relate to comparisons of original documents, warrant deference because the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage.

The Appellants argue that no samples of these officials documents were before the RPD and that it is unfair to compare two different types of certificate rather than, for example, two birth certificates. I do not find this persuasive, since the documents are purportedly issued by the same organization, yet important features such as crests, logos, and stamps are different.

Counsel also argues, conversely, that objective documentation "actually confirms the form and content of the summons." Given that no summons is at issue in this case, and that counsel also argues that there are no sample documents in evidence, this argument is not responsive to the facts before me.

The Appellants also argue that the stamps are not, in fact, different, but rather one was faded and unclear. Having compared the copies of the documents, I agree with the RPD that the stamps look different, and one has a spelling mistake in it while the other does not: Registry versus Regisry. However, even if I accepted this argument, it does not explain the significant other differences noted.

Finally, the death certificate issued XXXX XXXX, 2003 lists the "Usual Place of Residence of the Deceased" as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Lagos - the Principal Appellant testified that the family did not live at this address until 2007.17 The Appellants argue that there was no evidence about when the document was obtained and that this might account for the difference. I do not see how this would account for why XXXX would be listed as living at an address that the family only moved to in 2007, since the document was issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2003.

I have reviewed the evidence on this matter. When asked to explain why the deceased was listed as living at an address she never resided, the Principal Appellant stated that he was building a house at this address and used it as a permanent address because he rented elsewhere.18 I note that the RPD erred in not evaluating whether this was a reasonable explanation. I have reviewed it, and I do not find this reasonably accounts for the discrepancy. The Principal Appellant made no mention of using this as a permanent address prior to 2007 until confronted with a significant discrepancy in the evidence. Given the other credibility concerns with the death certificate as well, I do not find there to have been a reasonable explanation for the use of this address on the death certificate.

Finally, the Appellants cite case law for the principle that a reason is required, beyond the general availability of false documents, to rebut the presumption that documents issued by a foreign government are valid. In this case, I find there is ample evidence to rebut this presumption. The RPD did not err in finding that the birth and death certificates were fraudulent on a balance of probabilities. Medical report
The Appellants presented a medical report relating to XXXX death. The RPD found that the report was fraudulent. The Appellants argue that this was in error.

The copy of the report submitted prior to the hearing19 listed a different address for the Appellants than the original medical report that was presented at the hearing.20 The address of the hospital also differed between the copy and the original. The Principal Appellant testified that his previous lawyer had instructed him to obtain an updated medical report with his most recent address in Nigeria, and that he did so in 2015 - this was the original he presented. He did not keep the original of the first report submitted.21

The "updated" report, however, is still dated the same as the first - February 20, 2003 - and not 2015. There is no indication on the document that it was reissued, and as the RPD noted the signature, stamp, and smudges are in the exact same place. Given that nothing in the document coincided with the explanation of a re-issued document, the RPD found that the document was fraudulent. I find no error in this analysis.

The RPD had no advantage in reading the contents of the report, and I have applied a standard of correctness to those features, as well as in assessing the Appellants' explanation. I have deferred to the RPD's meaningful advantage when comparing features such as smudges and stamps on original documents and found this analysis reasonable.

The Appellants also argue that the fact of having presented the two reports increases their credibility, as they could have chosen to submit but one. I disagree. While in some cases, an admission against interest may be credible, in this case there is nothing about the second report to support the testimony that it is an update. Rather, both documents purport to be genuine documents issued in 2003 - with different addresses for the patient and different addresses for the hospital. The discrepancy was not reasonably explained. Moreover, as above, the second report lists the same Lagos address, in a document purporting to have been issued in 2003, at which the Appellants did not live until 2007.

The Appellants argue that it is possible that the hospital changed locations between 2003 when the first report was issued and 2015 when the second one was issued. This amounts to pure conjecture - there is no evidence that the hospital moved.

I agree with the RPD that the differences between the two versions of the same document are not reasonably explained, and that they are therefore not genuine documents on a balance of probabilities. Omission from immigration applications

The Appellants did not list XXXX on question five of the BOC, which specifically asks for relatives, including children, "living or dead." They submitted two amendments to their BOC, the second of which was to add Ifeoma as a relative. The RPD found that they had not provided a reasonable explanation.

The Appellants now argue that this was microscopic. They argue that they had difficulty initially submitting these forms and that their first counsel had made several errors in their completion - it was present counsel who assisted with this amendment. They also argue that they were in a "Catch 22 position" because they would otherwise have been faulted for not amending their BOC.

When asked why they had not initially listed their first daughter in their BOC, the Principal Appellant testified that he had given all of the information to his lawyer at the time and that they were not given much time to review it before signing.22 I do not find this to be a reasonable explanation, and find no error in the RPD's rejection of it. The Principal Appellant is a sophisticated man - while he may not have completed a high level of education, he owned and operated a successful fuel supply business himself for eight years, supervising five employees and supplying diesel to twenty different companies.23 He speaks English. The question specifically asked for the Appellants to list deceased relatives as well.

I also note that the Appellants made no mention of their first daughter on their visa application to Canada. The Principal Appellant testified that this was because culturally they do not list the dead among the living, that it brought back sad memories to think about her, and that he had not read over the forms that the agent prepared before he signed them. I do not find this to be a reasonable explanation for the same reasons as above.

The RPD also found the omission to be incongruent with the Principal Appellant's testimony that his daughter's death was fresh in his memory. The Appellants now argue that it was the RPD's questioning about the incident that made the memories fresh. I do not find this to be an important element of the analysis.

Rather, when the evidence is weighed together along with the grave problems with the documentation submitted, I find that the omission of any mention of their deceased daughter in listing their family members on immigration forms weighs against the Appellants - they have not established her life or death on a balance of probabilities. The police reports are not genuine

The RPD considered the three police reports the Appellants submitted. On the basis of discrepancies, the RPD found that the reports were not genuine, and drew a negative inference against the Appellants' credibility.

In evaluating the colour and visual features of original documents not before me, I find that the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in assessing their credibility. I find that the RPD's findings are therefore owed deference. These findings have been evaluated on a RAD reasonableness standard.

First, the RPD found that the appearances of the reports, in terms of colouring of the letterhead and the appearance of the police logo, varied inexplicably between three documents purportedly issued from the same police station. The Appellants have not advanced a clear argument as to how this finding is in error, except to state that there must be a valid reason to rebut the presumption that government issued documents are valid.24 In this case, the RPD referred to objective documentary evidence that the police logo in Nigeria does not vary across the country.25 Two of the three logos on the police reports had a garland, while the sample logo in the objective documentary evidence did not.26 Moreover, the colouring between the first two reports, which were issued more than 12 years apart, was similar, and different than the third report, issued only 8 months after the second report. I find that the RPD clearly explained a valid reason to rebut the presumption, and I accept that this was a reasonable analysis.

The RPD also found that the same officer was purported to have signed the second two reports, DSP XXXX XXXX, but that the signatures on the reports are different.27 The Appellants argue that the signatures are not different. Again, I defer to the RPD Member, who was able to review the original documents. The signatures are not wildly different, but they do differ particularly in the final letter or upstroke. Were this the only reason to doubt the authenticity of the reports, I would have found that it was insufficient. As part of a series of reasons, however, I find that the RPD's analysis was reasonable in the RAD context.

The RPD also found it to be contradictory that the Principal Appellant indicated in his BOC that when he reported the circumcision of his first daughter and the threat of the same to his second daughter, the police "said it was tradition" and that they "had no business getting involved,"28 while the police had allegedly provided long, detailed reports. The RPD did not find the explanation that the police had to provide reports in response to his complaints to reasonably account for the Principal Appellant's statement in his BOC that the police would not get involved. The Appellants now argue that the BOC stated that everything was reported to police and that it was after the Principal Appellant made a report that the police indicated they would not take action - they argue that there is no contradiction. I disagree. The 2003 report indicates that the police conducted an investigation and closed the case - this is distinct from the allegation in the BOC that "the Nigerian Police does nothing about" female circumcision.29 Moreover, female genital mutilation is banned in Nigeria, though actual implementation of the ban is not effective30 - it is therefore not credible that the police issued these reports, particularly the report of 31 May 2015, stating that no action was necessary because it was a traditional matter. While ineffective policing would account for police doing nothing or refusing to act, documenting their lack of diligence in their responsibilities is far different. This specific finding about the police reports was reviewed on a standard of correctness, since the RPD enjoyed no meaningful advantage.

Finally, the RAD also notes that the address listed on the 2003 police report is, as explained above, the Lagos address that the Appellants did not move to until 2007. I find that this further calls the authenticity of that report into question.

Therefore, I do not find that the RPD erred in finding that the police reports were not genuine documents, on a balance of probabilities. I agree that this reflects negatively on the Appellants' credibility. The testimony regarding the brother's arrest was inconsistent

The RPD also found that the Principal Appellant's testimony about his brother's arrest for homosexuality contained a significant inconsistency about who was present. The Appellants now argue that the RPD failed to evaluate his explanation and that the female Appellant confirmed his testimony. The Appellants argue that the RPD's finding was microscopic.

The Principal Appellant's BOC alleges that while being pressured by his Uncle XXXX to circumcise his daughter, there was a commotion outside. When the adult Appellants and Uncle XXXX went outside, they witnessed the Principal Appellant's brother being arrested for homosexuality. At the hearing, the Principal Appellant testified spontaneously, when describing the incident, that it had been his wife and Chief XXXX who was with him at this time.31 He was asked again who was with him, and he testified that he and his wife were with Chief XXXX.32 Later, he was asked whether or not the chief was still there when the Principal Appellant called his family, and he testified that he was, quoted what the chief had said, and confirmed that he witnessed the whole episode.33 This testimony was confirmed a fourth time.34

The Principal Appellant was then asked where his Uncle XXXX was during this time, and he testified that he did not know where Uncle XXXX was at the time but that he was not with them.35 Only when he was asked whether he had spoken to Uncle XXXX about the situation did the Principal Appellant begin to recant, eventually testifying that Uncle XXXX said the things he had originally attributed to Chief XXXX and that those present were Uncle XXXX and the adult Appellants.36 His explanation for the discrepancy is that he was experiencing flashbacks, his memory was disorganized, and that because of Chief XXXX terrible role in the threats to his family his name was always in the Principal Appellant's head and on his lips.37

The RPD did not find that this reasonably accounted for the discrepancy, and I agree. The Appellants argue that this was an understandable mix up which he corrected when he realized it. The Principal Appellant did not correct himself after a slip of the tongue - he confirmed four times that Chief XXXX was there, and then further testified that Uncle XXXX was not before altering his testimony. While flashbacks, or ruminations on an agent of persecution might account for a mistake, the Principal Appellant confirmed a specific, detailed set of events which, as the RPD noted, he claimed to remember "vividly." A mix up, as the Appellants now argue, does not reasonably account for the extent of the contradiction.

The Appellants also argue that the female Appellant testified that it was Uncle XXXX who was present, and that this lends credibility or corroboration to the allegation. I do not find this argument persuasive. First, the female Appellant was present for her husband's testimony and his confrontation with the contradiction it contained. Her corroboration of what was in the BOC is not overly probative since she was aware of the credibility concern that had arisen.

The events of the day in question are central to the claim - the day after the Appellant's daughter was threatened with circumcision and the day that the Principal Appellant became at risk because of his brother's alleged arrest for homosexuality. I do not find that the RPD's finding was microscopic, as the Appellants now argue. Rather, having reviewed the testimony, I have the impression that the Appellants were trying to testify to something memorized rather than a lived experience - their testimony did not have the ring of truth to it in light of the significant contradictions. The RPD was correct in finding this weighed against the Appellants' credibility. The supporting affidavits are insufficient and unreliable

The Appellants submitted five affidavits from affiants in Nigeria in support of their claims.38 The affidavits attest to various parts of the Appellants' allegations, but all five specifically mention that the Principal Appellant's brother was arrested for homosexuality and that this has cast police suspicion on the Principal Appellant himself. Several attest to helping and/or informing the Principal Appellant of police efforts to locate him and how he has evaded them. One affidavit was sworn at a Notary Public in the Judicial Division, while another was at the High Court of Lagos State, Ikeja Division. The rest claim to have been sworn before lawyers or notaries.

The RPD found that the affidavits were not genuine and assigned them no weight. Objective documentary evidence indicates that swearing an affidavit of this nature could well place the affiant in danger, since homosexuality is illegal and, as the Appellants allege, assisting homosexuals is dangerous.

The Appellants argue that the objective evidence in question "suggests that there would not be need for such affidavits to be deposed to or used locally in Nigeria" and that therefore these affidavits "are to be used abroad."39 I do not find this to be an accurate characterization of the evidence. It is true that the research in question quotes sources as saying that affidavits attesting to an individual's homosexuality are not used in Nigeria. It also indicates, however, that it is dangerous to the affiant to swear such an affidavit, that no source consulted was aware of this being done, and that [h]igh levels of homophobia and the criminalization of same-sex practice and relationships would prevent LGBT individuals or allies from swearing such an affidavit with a Nigerian notary public/commissioner of oaths. They would likely fear outing (which can lead to loss of family, friends, work, education), violence, arrest, blackmail and extortion. The Nigerian notary public/commissioner of oaths may also refuse to participate in such an activity due to the same homophobia and criminalization.40

The argument that an affidavit intended for use outside of Nigeria would somehow not be subject to this same violence and stigma is not persuasive, particularly where some of the affidavits in question were sworn in public fora such as a court. I find, as did the RPD, it to be implausible that the affiants in question would implicate themselves as knowing about the Principal Appellant and his brother's homosexuality, much less specifically attest to aiding and abetting a fugitive from police to avoid being caught. It is implausible that a commissioner would assist in commissioning such an affidavit. I also find, as the RPD did, that the Appellants' use of other fraudulent documents, taken together with the implausible nature of these documents, renders it more likely than not that the affidavits are also fraudulently obtained.
I therefore find that the RPD was correct in its assessment of this evidence. I also do not find it deserving of weight. The psychological report does not remedy the credibility problems

The RPD considered the report of Dr. XXXX regarding the Principal Appellant,41 but found that its probative value was diminished since it was based upon evidence that the RPD had not found to be credible. The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to assess what impact the diagnosis contained in the report may have had on his ability to testify. I agree that though the RPD was entitled to disbelieve the source of the Principal Appellant's symptoms, it was incumbent upon the RPD to consider how the symptoms might account for difficulties in testimony.

Though this analysis was wanting in the RPD's decision, I have considered the report and I do not find that it reasonably accounts for the Appellants' credibility problems. Of course, the report does not account for the irregularities in the Appellants supporting documentation, nor the supportable negative inference drawn for having submitted fraudulent documents. The Appellants argue that the mention of intrusive ideation, mind going blank, forgetting someone's name, or being forgetful and distracted might account for the why the Principal Appellant mixed up who was present when his brother was arrested: Chief XXXX or Uncle XXXX. I do not find this to be the case. While it might have explained some difficulties, such as mentioned in the report (an inability to recall details on the spot, the need for frequent breaks, or questions to be rephrased), I do not find that it accounts for the Principal Appellant's presentation of a detailed, cohesive story about Chief XXXX and his actions, presented as a clear memory, or his initial testimony that Uncle XXXX was not there. Having reviewed the record, this is distinct from forgetting someone's name, or missing your subway stop.

In the circumstances of this case, Dr. XXXX' diagnosis of the Principal Appellant with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX with prolonged duration does not explain or outweigh the credibility problems with the Appellants' evidence.
For the above reasons, I find that the RPD did not err in rejecting the Appellants' claims for want of credibility.

I have also considered, since there are minor Appellants, each appeal individually on its merits. In this case, having found the allegations that the minor Appellants face circumcision or harmful traditional rituals not to be credible, and since no other grounds of risk to the minor Appellants arise from their personal circumstances, I do not find that there is any basis to determine the minor Appellants' appeals differently than those of their parents.

I therefore confirm the determination of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.
